Discrete probability distribution

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Probability and statistics Probability theory Probability distribution
OurBigBook.com Words: 7k Articles: 80
A discrete probability distribution is a probability distribution concentrated on a finite or countable set of possible values S: a random variable X with this law satisfies P(X∈S)=1. Its probability mass function assigns a probability to each value:
pX​(x)=P(X=x),pX​(x)≥0,∑x∈S​pX​(x)=1.
(1)
Thus the probability of an event is obtained by adding masses, rather than integrating a probability density function. The possible values need not be equally spaced, or even integers. When the relevant moments are finite, its expected value and variance are
μ=EX=∑x∈S​xpX​(x),Var(X)=∑x∈S​(x−μ)2pX​(x)=E[X2]−μ2.
(2)
For a constructed example, assign values 0,2,5 masses 0.5,0.3,0.2. They sum to one; P(X≥2)=0.3+0.2=0.5, EX=0(0.5)+2(0.3)+5(0.2)=1.6, and E[X2]=4(0.3)+25(0.2)=6.2. Hence the variance is 6.2−1.62=3.64. A mean can lie between possible values: no outcome here equals 1.6.
The useful organizing question is what an experiment records. One yes/no indicator random variable gives a Bernoulli distribution; a success count in a fixed number of independent attempts gives a binomial distribution; the attempt number of the first success gives a geometric distribution. A Poisson distribution describes an event count under different assumptions. Naming the quantity first helps prevent selecting a familiar formula for the wrong experiment.

Benford law (P(D=d)=log10​(1+1/d))

Words: 918 Articles: 4
Discrete probability distribution OurBigBook.com
For a positive random variable X, let D∈{1,…,9} be its first nonzero base-ten digit. The Benford law is the discrete probability distribution with probability mass function
P(D=d)=log10​(dd+1​)=log10​(1+1/d),d=1,…,9.
(3)
Here X need not be an integer: 0.0042, 4.2 and 4200 all have D=4. Multiplication by an integer power of ten changes the decimal point's position and leaves the first nonzero digit unchanged. Zero has no first nonzero digit, so exclude it. For negative inputs one may explicitly use their absolute values, still excluding zero; that convention must be stated rather than applying a logarithm to a negative number.
The Benford law favors small digits: P(D=1)=log10​2≈0.301029996, whereas P(D=9)=log10​(10/9)≈0.04575749. Thus the model assigns about 30.10% to digit one and 4.58% to digit nine. The masses are positive and their normalization is a finite telescoping series:
∑d=19​P(D=d)=∑d=19​(log10​(d+1)−log10​d)=log10​10−log10​1=1.
(4)
Why can digit one be so common? In a decimal significand interval [1,10), the digit-one region [1,2) occupies a larger fraction of the logarithmic scale than the digit-nine region [9,10). The precise assumption is that the fractional part of the base-ten logarithm is distributed uniformly on [0,1); Benford law from logarithmic uniformity turns those unequal interval lengths into probabilities. This makes a surprising digit pattern into a simple geometry of multiplicative size. The logarithmic explanation is also presented in Peter Sheridan Dodds, Benford's Law, essential story.
The Benford law is useful as a proposed model for leading digits when the mechanism supports logarithmic uniformity or an appropriate limiting argument, such as Benford frequencies for powers of an integer. Merely spanning many powers of ten does not establish that assumption. A discrepancy from the Benford law can prompt investigation of the model and data collection; by itself it does not establish fraud, and agreement does not establish authenticity.
Simon Newcomb's 1881 paper, Note on the Frequency of Use of the Different Digits in Natural Numbers, appeared in the American Journal of Mathematics 4, pp. 39–40. Its opening connects unequal leading-digit frequencies with the faster wear of early pages in logarithm tables. The publication metadata and original opening excerpt are available in Newcomb (1881), original publication record and [ref]. Frank Benford's The Law of Anomalous Numbers, Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society 78 (1938), pp. 551–572, likewise discusses worn logarithm tables on p. 551 and tabulates observations on p. 553. See Benford (1938), transcription of the original paper with page numbers and publication metadata. These observations motivated study of the digit pattern; they do not make the Benford law universal.

Scale invariance of decimal significands

Words: 121 Articles: 1
Benford law OurBigBook.com
A decimal significand lies in [1,10), obtained by removing the integer power of ten from a positive number. Multiplication by a constant rotates the fractional logarithm modulo one. Invariance under every such rotation makes the fractional logarithm uniform and hence implies Benford law. This is an invariant significand distribution, not a proper scale-invariant distribution for the entire positive number.

Decimal significand (S10​(x)=10{log10​x})

Words: 62
Scale invariance of decimal significands OurBigBook.com
For x>0, the decimal significand is the unique S10​(x)∈[1,10) such that x=10kS10​(x) for an integer k. Explicitly, k=⌊log10​x⌋ and S10​(x)=10{log10​x}, using the floor function and the fractional part. For 0.0042, 4.2 and 4200, the decimal significand is 4.2 and the first nonzero digit is ⌊S10​(x)⌋=4. In the classical terminology of logarithm tables, the logarithmic mantissa is {log10​x}, which differs from the decimal significand 10{log10​x}.

Benford law from logarithmic uniformity (P(D=i)=log10​(1+1/i))

Words: 350
Benford law OurBigBook.com
For a positive random variable X, write its base-ten logarithm as an integer part plus a fractional part:
K=⌊log10​X⌋,Z={log10​X}=log10​X−K∈[0,1),X=10K10Z.
(5)
The floor function handles values below one as well: for X=0.0042, K=−3 and the decimal significand is 10Z=4.2. Since 10Z∈[1,10), the first nonzero decimal digit is D=⌊10Z⌋. The monotonicity of the logarithm gives the exact event equivalence
D=d⟺d≤10Z<d+1⟺log10​d≤Z<log10​(d+1).
(6)
If Z has the uniform distribution on [0,1), the probability of this interval is its length. Consequently P(D=d)=log10​(d+1)−log10​d, proving the Benford law. This argument assumes uniformity of the fractional part of the logarithm, rather than uniformity of X itself. See the logarithmic-coordinate explanation in Peter Sheridan Dodds, Benford's Law, essential story.
An exact constructed example is the log-uniform distribution on [1,10), with probability density function fX​(x)=1/(xln10) there and zero elsewhere. Its total mass is ∫110​dx/(xln10)=1. The change of variables formula with x=10z gives fZ​(z)=fX​(10z)(ln10)10z=1 for 0≤z<1. Equivalently, integrating directly gives
P(D=d)=∫dd+1​xln10dx​=ln10ln(d+1)−lnd​=log10​(dd+1​).
(7)
For example, the probability of first digit four is log10​(5/4)≈0.096910013. By contrast, an ordinary uniform distribution for X on [1,10) has probability density function 1/9 there, so P(D=d)=∫dd+1​dx/9=1/9 for every digit. This is a concrete counterexample to any claim that the Benford law holds for every positive random variable.
More generally, a log-uniform distribution on [A,B) with 0<A<B has uniform Y=log10​X on [log10​A,log10​B). If its logarithmic span log10​(B/A)=m is a positive integer, reduction to the fractional part wraps an interval of length m around the unit interval exactly m times, making Z uniform even when A is not a power of ten. Arbitrary partial-decade truncations generally do not have this property: for a log-uniform distribution on [1,2), the first digit is always one.
Under the uniform fractional-logarithm assumption, multiplication by any constant c>0 replaces Z by Z′={Z+log10​c}. This is a rotation modulo one, which preserves the uniform distribution and therefore preserves the Benford law; see scale invariance of decimal significands. For the constructed [1,10) example, multiplying by 0.001 gives a log-uniform distribution on [0.001,0.01) with the same digit probabilities. The claim concerns the decimal significand law: there is no proper probability density function proportional to 1/x over all of (0,∞), since its integral diverges. The existing scale-invariant prior describes that unnormalizable measure, while a finite log-uniform distribution is normalizable.

Benford frequencies for powers of an integer

Words: 46
Benford law OurBigBook.com
If a≥2 is an integer with irrational log10​a, then the leading digit d of an has limiting frequency log10​(1+1/d). Indeed the logarithmic fractional parts are the orbit of zero under an irrational rotation of the circle, so everywhere interval frequency under an irrational rotation applies. Thus for a=2, digit seven has frequency (log8−log7)/log10.

Bernoulli distribution (Bernoulli(p))

Words: 376 Articles: 3
Discrete probability distribution OurBigBook.com
A Bernoulli random variable records one success as 1 and one failure as 0. For 0≤p≤1, its probability mass function is
P(B=1)=p,P(B=0)=1−p,
(8)
with zero mass elsewhere. The terms success and failure merely name outcomes; success need not be desirable. Any event A produces such a variable through its indicator random variable B=1A​, with p=P(A). A single Bernoulli distribution requires no independence assumption; independence becomes relevant when several trials are combined.
Because B2=B, the expected value and variance follow immediately:
EB=0(1−p)+1p=p,Var(B)=E[B2]−(EB)2=p−p2=p(1−p).
(9)
For a constructed trial with p=0.3, these are 0.3 and 0.21. The variance is greatest at p=1/2, where it equals 1/4, since p(1−p)=1/4−(p−1/2)2. At p=0 or p=1, the outcome is certain and the variance vanishes.
The beauty of an indicator random variable is that counting becomes addition: summing such indicators counts successes, and the linearity of expectation gives the expected count even when the indicators are dependent. With independence and a shared p, the full count law is the binomial distribution. These models are summarized in Penn State STAT 504, discrete distributions.
A historical anchor is Bernoulli's posthumous Ars conjectandi: its original title page identifies the author and records publication at Basel in 1713. This documents the book's publication, rather than establishing priority for the modern name Bernoulli distribution. See Ars conjectandi, original title page, ETH Library.

Estimating Bernoulli variance (ϕ=θ(1−θ))

Words: 76
Bernoulli distribution OurBigBook.com
For n≥2 independent Bernoulli observations with sum K, the extended maximum-likelihood estimator is ϕ​=(K/n)(1−K/n). Its unbiased improvement is K(n−K)/[n(n−1)]=nϕ​/(n−1), obtained by conditioning X1​(1−X2​) on K. The Rao-Blackwell theorem gives strict variance reduction for 0<θ<1. With a uniform prior on θ and squared-error loss for ϕ, the Bayes estimator is (K+1)(n−K+1)/[(n+2)(n+3)]. For parameter space strictly (0,1), samples with K=0 or n have only a boundary likelihood supremum, not an attained maximum.

Bernoulli trial (X∼Bernoulli(θ))

Words: 47
Bernoulli distribution OurBigBook.com
A random experiment with two outcomes, success and failure, whose success indicator has a Bernoulli distribution. Repeated trials sharing success probability θ give a binomial distribution for their success count if they are independent conditional on θ; integrating over an uncertain common θ generally makes the trials dependent marginally.

Bernoulli thinning

Words: 37
Bernoulli distribution OurBigBook.com
If an event occurs with probability p and is independently retained with conditional probability q, its retained indicator is Bernoulli with probability pq. Applying this independently to a binomial count turns Binomial(n,p) into Binomial(n,pq).

Geometric distribution (Geom(p))

Words: 763 Articles: 8
Discrete probability distribution OurBigBook.com
Consider successive independent Bernoulli trials with the same success probability 0<p≤1. A geometric distribution models waiting for their first success. Two conventions coexist, so always say what is counted. Let T count all trials up to and including the successful trial, and let F=T−1 count preceding failures. Their probability mass functions are
P(T=k)=(1−p)k−1p,k=1,2,…,P(F=j)=(1−p)jp,j=0,1,….
(10)
The factors describe failures followed by one success; independence permits multiplication. Summing the geometric series verifies that each law has total mass one. Their expected values differ by one, while shifting by a constant leaves the variance unchanged:
ET=p1​,EF=p1−p​,Var(T)=Var(F)=p21−p​.
(11)
The positive convention and these moments are also given in Penn State STAT 414, geometric distributions.
For a constructed retry mechanism with independent attempts and p=0.3, success on attempt four has probability P(T=4)=0.73(0.3)=0.1029. More than four attempts are needed precisely when the first four fail: P(T>4)=0.74=0.2401. The expected values are ET=10/3 and EF=7/3, and the common variance is 70/9≈7.7778. The large spread explains why the average waiting count is not a deadline.
The striking memorylessness of the geometric distribution says that, for nonnegative integers m,r with P(T>m)>0,
P(T>m+r∣T>m)=(1−p)m(1−p)m+r​=(1−p)r=P(T>r).
(12)
After five failures, the conditional probability of requiring more than two additional attempts is still 0.72=0.49. The analogous zero-based identity uses P(F≥m+r∣F≥m)=P(F≥r); keeping the inequalities straight avoids an off-by-one error. This property follows from fresh independent trials with unchanged p; learning or changing conditions can destroy it. At p=0, success never occurs, so there is no proper finite waiting-count law.

Memorylessness of the geometric distribution (P(T>m+r∣T>m)=P(T>r))

Words: 71
Geometric distribution OurBigBook.com
For the positive-integer geometric distribution with success probability 0<p≤1, the displayed identity holds for nonnegative integers m,r whenever the conditioning event has positive probability. The first m attempts have failed; future independent attempts use the same success probability. Equivalently, divide the tail (1−p)m+r by (1−p)m. For a zero-based failures count F=T−1, use P(F≥m+r∣F≥m)=P(F≥r). Constant success probability and independence are essential: accumulated wear or learning would require a different model.

Geometric return count before absorption (K∼Geom(Pi​(absorption before return to i)))

Words: 73
Geometric distribution OurBigBook.com
Start a Markov chain at a nonabsorbing state i. If each departure from i has probability p>0 of absorption before the next return, the Strong Markov property makes the number of visits to i, including the initial one, a positive-integer geometric random variable of parameter p. For a continuous-time Markov chain whose holding times at i are independent rate-λi​ exponentials, independently of the embedded jump chain, the total occupation time at i is a sum of K such holding times and has expected value 1/(pλi​).

Geometric count under Bernoulli thinning (pα​=p/(p+(1−p)α))

Words: 54
Geometric distribution OurBigBook.com
Independently retain each event of a zero-based geometric distribution count with probability α. Conditional on the original count, the retained count is binomial, so its probability generating function is p/[1−(1−p)(1−α+αz)]. This is again a zero-based geometric distribution, with success parameter pα​ and mean α(1−p)/p. In excess of loss reinsurance, α is the probability that a claim exceeds the retention.

GX​(s)=p∑j=1k−1​qj−1sj+qk−1sk,EX=p1−qk​.

Poissonized coupon completion time and count (λET=EL)

Words: 72
Coupon collector problem OurBigBook.com
For independent coupon labels arriving at rate λ, Poisson thinning makes the type-specific first arrival times independent exponentials of rates λpj​. Completion time is their maximum. Its distribution is P(T<t)=∏j​(1−e−λpj​t). The completion count L depends only on the labels and is independent of the exponential interarrival sequence. Therefore T=∑k≥1​Ek​1{L≥k}​ and nonnegative integration gives the displayed identity. Completion count and its expectation do not depend on arrival rate.

Waiting time to observe both Bernoulli outcomes (EN=p(1−p)1​−1)

Words: 82
Coupon collector problem OurBigBook.com
In independent trials with two outcomes of probabilities p and q=1−p, let N include the first trial and the trial that first completes the pair. Conditional on the first outcome, N−1 has a geometric distribution of parameter q or p, with mixture weights p,q. The law of total expectation and law of total variance give
EN=1+qp​+pq​=pq1​−1,VarN=q2p2​+p2q2​+pq(p−q)2​=p2q21​−pq3​−2.
(16)
The final term in the unsimplified variance is the variance of the two conditional means; omitting it is incorrect unless p=q. Both outcomes must have positive probability for these finite formulas.

Coupon collector waiting-time variance (Var(T)=n2∑r=1n​r−2−n∑r=1n​r−1)

Words: 61
Coupon collector problem OurBigBook.com
For uniform independent draws of n coupon types, the waiting times with r unseen types remaining are independent positive-support geometric distributions of parameter r/n. Summing their means gives n∑r=1n​1/r, and summing their variances gives the displayed formula. Independence follows from fresh draws after each discovery and the fact that the next stage's conditional distribution depends only on the count of remaining types.

Negative binomial distribution

Words: 738 Articles: 2
Discrete probability distribution OurBigBook.com
The negative binomial distribution counts failures before a target number of successes in successive independent Bernoulli trials with constant success probability p. In this stopping model, r is a positive integer and 0<p≤1. On the failures-before-the-rth-success convention, the random variable X takes values 0,1,…; for 0<p<1, its probability mass function is
P(X=x)=(xx+r−1​)(1−p)xpr,x=0,1,….
(17)
The binomial coefficient counts possible arrangements before the final success, as explained by the negative binomial stopping argument. At p=1, every trial succeeds: X=0 with probability one, so its expected value and variance are both zero. This handles the endpoint without needing to interpret 00. At p=0, the target is never reached and there is no proper finite waiting-count law.
For a worked example, toss a fair coin until the second head, calling heads S and tails F. Thus r=2 and p=1/2. Exactly two failures means that the second success is on trial four. The complete stopped sequences are SFFS, FSFS and FFSS; each has probability (1/2)4=1/16, giving P(X=2)=3/16. The first three masses are
P(X=0)=41​,P(X=1)=41​,P(X=2)=163​.
(18)
Both 0 and 1 are modes, each with mass 1/4: there is no unique mode here. Later masses decrease, since P(X=x+1)/P(X=x)=(x+2)/(2x+2)<1 for x≥1.
The expected value and variance of the failures count are
EX=pr(1−p)​,Var(X)=p2r(1−p)​.
(19)
If instead N=X+r counts all trials, including the r successes, then N≥r and
EN=pr​,Var(N)=p2r(1−p)​.
(20)
For the fair-coin example, EX=2, Var(X)=4, and EN=4. Shifting the count changes its expected value but preserves its variance. When r=1, X has the failures-count geometric distribution, while N=X+1 has the all-trials geometric distribution. The two conventions and the moments are treated in Kyle Siegrist, The Negative Binomial Distribution, Random Services.
The negative binomial distribution is useful when a procedure runs until it collects a target number of successes: for example, obtaining r usable samples from independent attempts with a stable acceptance probability. A binomial distribution instead counts successes in a fixed number of trials. The attractive connection is that these two experimental questions can be answered from the same trial sequence, using the negative binomial stopping argument. For the failures count and 0<p<1, the positive mean μ=r(1−p)/p satisfies Var(X)=μ/p>μ, so the law allows overdispersion relative to a Poisson distribution. At p=1, both quantities vanish and the inequality is not strict. The separate Poisson-gamma mixture explains another way this count law arises; its noninteger shape parameters do not represent a literal target number of successes.

Negative binomial stopping argument

Words: 290
Negative binomial distribution OurBigBook.com
For the negative binomial distribution with positive integer target r and success probability 0<p<1, the rth success occurs after exactly x failures only if the final trial is a success, while the preceding x+r−1 trials contain x failures and r−1 successes. Choosing the failure locations gives the binomial coefficient (xx+r−1​). Each such stopped sequence has probability (1−p)xpr by independence, and the sequences describe mutually exclusive events, so their probabilities add. This proves the probability mass function. Counting arrangements among all x+r positions would wrongly include sequences that already reached the target earlier. The same argument is used for three heads in MIT 18.05, spring 2022, problem set 9 solutions, problem 2(b).
A short route to normalization and moments is to split the failures count into successive waiting blocks:
X=F1​+⋯+Fr​,
(21)
where Fi​ counts failures after success i−1 and before success i, with F1​ starting at the first trial. Fresh independent Bernoulli trials make the blocks independent, each with the failures-count geometric distribution. Each block has total mass p∑j=0∞​(1−p)j=1 by the geometric series, so their sum also defines a normalized probability distribution. The linearity of expectation and variance additivity for independent random variables give EX=r(1−p)/p and Var(X)=r(1−p)/p2. This makes the moments transparent without a long calculation of sums. For p=1, every block is zero.
The same stopping rule connects a waiting count to a fixed-length count. Let N=X+r be the trial number of the rth success, and let Bn​ count successes in the first n trials, so Bn​ has a binomial distribution. For any nonnegative integer n,
{N>n}={Bn​<r},P(N>n)=∑k=0min(r−1,n)​(kn​)pk(1−p)n−k.
(22)
The target is still unmet after n trials exactly when fewer than r successes have occurred. With r=2, p=1/2 and n=4, this gives P(N>4)=(1+4)/16=5/16; equivalently, P(X≤2)=1−5/16=11/16, matching 1/4+1/4+3/16. At p=1, the event identity still holds, with N=r and Bn​=n deterministically.

Binomial distribution (Bin(n,p))

Words: 641 Articles: 7
Discrete probability distribution OurBigBook.com
The binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number n of independent Bernoulli trials with common success probability p. Equivalently,
K=B1​+⋯+Bn​,Bi​∼Bernoulli(p),P(K=k)=(kn​)pk(1−p)n−k,k=0,…,n.
(24)
Here n is a nonnegative integer and 0≤p≤1. The binomial coefficient (kn​)=n!/[k!(n−k)!] counts placements of the k successes; each particular arrangement has probability pk(1−p)n−k. The binomial theorem makes the masses sum to [p+(1−p)]n=1. At p=0 all mass is at zero, and at p=1 all mass is at n; these endpoint laws can be read directly without interpreting 00.
The linearity of expectation and addition of variances for independent random variables give
EK=np,Var(K)=np(1−p).
(25)
The fixed trial count, common success probability, and joint independence are substantive model assumptions. Sampling uniformly without replacement from a finite population instead leads to a hypergeometric distribution. Independent trials with different success probabilities generally give a Poisson binomial distribution. Common marginal success probabilities alone are insufficient: if all ten indicators equal the same Bernoulli random variable with p=0.3, their sum is zero with probability 0.7 or ten with probability 0.3. Its mean is still three, but its variance is 100(0.21)=21. The standard construction is given in Penn State STAT 504, binomial distribution.
For an exact constructed example, let each of ten independent trials choose uniformly from ten labelled tokens, with replacement, and mark three tokens as successes. Then p=3/10 and K∼Bin(10,0.3). Exactly three successes have probability
P(K=3)=(310​)(0.3)3(0.7)7=120(0.027)(0.0823543)=0.266827932.

The mean is 10(0.3)=3, the variance is 10(0.3)(0.7)=2.1, and the standard deviation is 2.1​≈1.4491. Zero successes have probability 0.710=0.0282475249, so at least one success has probability 1−0.710=0.9717524751. A single count calculation replaces enumeration of all 1010 equally likely token sequences.
Each bar's height is one probability mass. Three is the most likely count, but its mass is only about 26.7%: a most likely outcome need not occur most of the time.

Words: 710 Articles: 2
Discrete probability distribution OurBigBook.com
The hypergeometric distribution counts marked objects in a uniformly chosen sample of fixed size from a finite population, using sampling without replacement. Let n≥1 be the population size, let 0≤c≤n objects be marked, and sample 0≤r≤n distinct objects. If K counts the marked objects selected, its probability mass function is
P(K=k)=(rn​)(kc​)(r−kn−c​)​,max(0,r−(n−c))≤k≤min(c,r).
(27)
The bounds describe the support of a probability distribution and k must be an integer; the mass is zero elsewhere. The denominator counts all size-r subsets, while the numerator counts choices of k marked and r−k unmarked objects using binomial coefficients. This counting argument requires every size-r sample to have the same probability.[ref]
For a constructed example, a box contains ten labelled objects, four red and six blue. Select five without replacement. There are (510​)=252 possible samples. The probabilities for K=0,1,2,3,4 are
421​,215​,2110​,215​,421​.
(28)
In particular, P(K=2)=(24​)(36​)/252=120/252=10/21. Five red objects are impossible because the box only contains four. The expected value is r(c/n)=2, and the variance is 2/3.
The count law also answers a detection question: what is the chance that five draws find at least one red object? By the complement rule of probability, it is 1−P(K=0)=41/42, approximately 0.9762. This can model inspecting five distinct objects from a known finite collection, with a mark indicating the property we want to detect. If repeated inspections can select the same object again, the replacement model instead gives 1−0.65=0.92224. Equal expected values therefore do not imply equal chances of detecting a marked object.
The corresponding binomial distribution counts red draws when each selected object is put back before the next independent draw: Krep​∼Bin(5,0.4). It has the same expected value 2, but variance 5(0.4)(0.6)=6/5, and it permits five red draws. Without replacement, a red first draw leaves red probability 3/9 for the next draw; a blue first draw leaves 4/9. This statistical dependence pulls the total toward the fixed composition of the population, producing the finite population correction.
The useful modelling question is whether previously selected objects remain available. A fixed-size sample of distinct items calls for a hypergeometric distribution; fresh independent trials with constant success probability call for a binomial distribution. When the population grows with c/n→p while r stays fixed, the hypergeometric masses tend to the corresponding binomial distribution masses: removing finitely many objects has an increasingly small effect on the next draw's probability.

In the ten-object, five-draw example, f2=5/9 and (6/5)(5/9)=2/3. The exceptional population size n=1 is deterministic and should be handled directly rather than inserting it into a zero denominator.

Words: 1k Articles: 10
Discrete probability distribution OurBigBook.com
A multinomial distribution describes category counts from n independent trials, each choosing exactly one of k categories with the same probabilities p1​,…,pk​. Require n≥0 to be an integer, pi​≥0, and ∑i​pi​=1. If Ni​ counts the trials in category i, then ∑i​Ni​=n and
P(N1​=n1​,…,Nk​=nk​)=n1​!⋯nk​!n!​∏i=1k​pini​​,ni​≥0,∑i​ni​=n.
(33)
The ni​ are integers, and the mass is zero for other count patterns. A category with pi​=0 has count zero almost surely, with 00=1 in this formula. For a specified ordered trial sequence, independence gives the product of numbers ∏i​pini​​; the multinomial coefficient counts the different sequences with that same count pattern.
For four trials with category probabilities (1/2,3/10,1/5), the count pattern (2,1,1) can occur in 4!/(2!1!1!)=12 orders, each of probability (1/2)2(3/10)(1/5)=0.015. Thus its total probability is 12(0.015)=0.18. This is a constructed independent-trial example, distinct from drawing four objects without replacement from a ten-object population of composition (5,3,2), where the multivariate hypergeometric distribution gives 2/7.
The diagram shows all fifteen possible count patterns. Coordinates (N1​,N2​) determine N3​=4−N1​−N2​; the triangle is a constraint on integer counts, not a continuous probability density. The mode is (N1​,N2​,N3​)=(2,1,1), where the probability mass function is largest, but the expected values (2,1.2,0.8) are not a possible count pattern.
Each single count has a binomial distribution, because recording category i versus all other categories reduces every trial to a Bernoulli trial. Consequently,
ENi​=npi​,Var(Ni​)=npi​(1−pi​),Cov(Ni​,Nj​)=−npi​pj​(i=j).
(34)
These statements about the joint count model are summarized in Aditya Guntuboyina's lecture notes.[ref]
Independent trials do not make the resulting counts independent random variables. Within one trial the indicator random variables for two distinct categories cannot both equal one, so their product is zero and their covariance is −pi​pj​. Summing over independent trials gives −npi​pj​. In the four-trial example, the variances are (1,0.84,0.64) and the pairwise covariances are −0.6,−0.4,−0.24. Knowing that all four trials were in the first category fixes the other two counts at zero.
The attraction is that one formula describes any fixed-total list of category counts while preserving the constraint that they add up to n. It underlies multinomial likelihood calculations and uniform balls-in-bins allocation. The multinomial aggregation rule lets us merge categories without leaving this family of probability distributions. Allowing independent category counts with an unfixed total instead leads to a different model, related through Poisson-multinomial conditioning.

For λ>0, a Poisson random variable N has probability mass function
P(N=k)=e−λk!λk​,k=0,1,2,…,EN=Var(N)=λ.

The exponential function series verifies normalization. At λ=0, define N=0 with certainty. The equality of mean and variance is a distinguishing model property, though it does not by itself characterize the law.
When counting events in a homogeneous Poisson process, distinguish its rate r from the distribution parameter: an interval of duration t has λ=rt. A rate measured per minute times a duration measured in minutes gives a dimensionless expected count. This process assumes independent increments, a constant rate, and a negligible chance of multiple events relative to interval length in a sufficiently short interval. A rate alone does not establish a Poisson distribution. See Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis, chapter 6 summary, pages 46-47.

P(N=0)=e−3≈0.0497871,P(N=3)=e−33!33​=4.5e−3≈0.2240418.

The probability of at least one event is 1−e−3≈0.9502129. These results describe the specified process, not every arrival mechanism with the same average rate.

The panels show the same count scale and the same Poisson distribution reference. At n=10, p=0.3 is not especially small and the difference is visible. No universal trial-count cutoff guarantees an adequate approximation for every event.
The independence assumption matters even when every success is rare. For n≥3, if all n indicator random variables equal one shared Bernoulli random variable of parameter 3/n, their sum is zero with probability 1−3/n and n with probability 3/n. Its mean is three, yet its zero-count probability tends to one, not e−3. Some dependent counts still admit approximation through the Stein-Chen method, but this requires additional control of dependence.

This bibliographic fact alone does not establish when the modern distribution terminology arose. See BnF record of Poisson's 1837 treatise.

A Poisson distribution of parameter a conditioned to lie in {0,…,C}. It is the occupancy law of a unit-resource loss network. Its mean is the carried load of an Erlang loss resource, a[1−E(C,a)]. Differentiating the mean with respect to loga gives its variance, which is positive for a>0 and C≥1; this proves strict monotonicity of the carried load.

Poisson mixture (Y∣Λ∼Poisson(Λ))

Words: 141 Articles: 3
Poisson distribution OurBigBook.com
A model with Y∣Λ∼Poisson(Λ) for a nonnegative random intensity. Conditional expectation and total variance give EY=EΛ and VarY=EΛ+VarΛ, explaining overdispersion. A Poisson-gamma mixture gives the negative binomial distribution.

Poisson-uniform posterior mean (E[Λ∣x1​,…,xn​]=∫lu​tse−ntdt∫lu​ts+1e−ntdt​)

Words: 40
Poisson mixture OurBigBook.com
For a uniform prior distribution on (l,u) with 0<l<u, conditionally independent Poisson distribution observations have sufficient count s=∑i​xi​. Their Bayesian posterior density is proportional to tse−nt on that bounded interval. The displayed posterior mean is the Bayes estimator under squared error loss, and is generally not the affine Bühlmann credibility estimate.

Shifted-exponential Poisson mixture (G(z)=eα(z−1)β/(β+1−z))

Words: 75 Articles: 1
Poisson mixture OurBigBook.com
When the random intensity is α+Y with Y having an exponential distribution of rate β, the mixed count is the sum of independent Poisson distribution and support-zero geometric distribution counts. The Poisson parameter is α and the geometric success probability is β/(β+1). At α=0 the law is geometric.
Shifted-exponential Poisson count recursion (n(β+1)pn​={n+α(β+1)}pn−1​−αpn−2​)
Words: 31
Shifted-exponential Poisson mixture OurBigBook.com
For the shifted-exponential Poisson mixture, the displayed relation holds for n≥2, initialized by p0​=e−αβ/(β+1) and p1​=(α+1/(β+1))p0​. It follows by differentiating the probability generating function and comparing coefficients. Nonnegativity follows from the independent Poisson-geometric convolution of independent random variables representation.

A Poisson distribution conditioned on a positive count has probability mass function P(Y=y)=θy/[y!(eθ−1)] for y≥1 and θ>0.

Parity estimator for a zero-truncated Poisson count

Words: 41
Zero-truncated Poisson distribution OurBigBook.com
For the zero-truncated Poisson distribution, 21{Y even}​ is the unique integrable nonrandomized unbiased estimator of p=1−e−θ. Indeed unbiasedness gives ∑y≥1​t(y)θy/y!=eθ+e−θ−2, and power series coefficients force the parity values. Its variance is 2p−p2; clipping it to 1{Y even}​ gives mean squared error p/2, strictly smaller for 0<p<1.

The sum of independent Poisson random variables is Poisson, with parameter equal to the sum of their parameters. This follows by multiplying their probability generating functions exp(λi​(z−1)).

For Bernoulli random variables X1​,…,Xn​, which need not be independent, put pi​=P(Xi​=1), S=∑i​Xi​, and λ=∑i​pi​. Then
De​(L(S)∥Poisson(λ))≤∑i​pi2​+∑i​He​(Xi​)−He​(X1​,…,Xn​).

The dependence penalty is the total correlation. The proof compares the joint Bernoulli law with the product of Poisson laws of means pi​, then applies the data processing inequality for relative entropy to addition.

A Poisson observation model represents a nonnegative count as conditionally Poisson with a mean supplied by an underlying process or regression model.

Poisson observation model OurBigBook.com
A Poisson observation is an integer-valued count modeled by a Poisson distribution of specified intensity, possibly conditionally on a latent field. Independent Poisson observations motivate Poisson data fidelity through their log-likelihood.

Zero-inflated Poisson distribution

Words: 288 Articles: 4
Poisson distribution OurBigBook.com
A zero-inflated Poisson distribution is a mixture of a point mass at zero and a Poisson distribution. If the Poisson component has weight π and mean λ, then its mean is πλ and its variance is πλ+π(1−π)λ2.

Zero-inflated Poisson regression (logμ=xTβ,logitπ=zTγ)

Words: 250 Articles: 3
Zero-inflated Poisson distribution OurBigBook.com
A zero-inflated Poisson regression specifies a structural-zero probability π and a susceptible-component Poisson distribution mean μ. In this parametrization,
P(Y=0)=π+(1−π)e−μ,P(Y=y)=(1−π)e−μμy/y!(y>0).
(44)
The mean is (1−π)μ. Logistic predictors for π and logarithmic predictors for μ allow covariates to affect component membership and count intensity differently. A susceptible individual can still generate a zero count; susceptibility is not equivalent to an observed positive response.
Posterior structural-zero probability (P(Z=1∣Y=0)=π+(1−π)e−μπ​)
Words: 47
Zero-inflated Poisson regression OurBigBook.com
In a zero-inflated Poisson regression, Bayes' theorem separates structural zeros from susceptible zero counts. A positive count rules out the structural-zero class; a zero raises its posterior probability according to the displayed formula, but usually does not determine class membership with certainty. This same probability supplies the E-step of the EM algorithm for zero-inflated Poisson regression.
Component and marginal effects in zero-inflated regression (E(Y)=(1−π)μ)
Words: 70
Zero-inflated Poisson regression OurBigBook.com
A logarithmic count-component contrast b multiplies the susceptible mean by eb, while a zero-logit contrast g multiplies the structural-zero odds by eg. If the baseline zero predictor is η, the marginal mean ratio is
eb1+eη+g1+eη​.
(45)
Thus the count ratio alone is not a population-average effect when a covariate changes both components. With interaction terms, the relevant count contrast must first include the interactions for the stated reference group.
EM algorithm for zero-inflated Poisson regression (τi​=P(Zi​=1∣Yi​))
Words: 71
Zero-inflated Poisson regression OurBigBook.com
The expectation-maximization algorithm introduces Zi​=1 for a structural zero. Its E-step gives τi​=0 at positive counts and τi​=πi​/[πi​+(1−πi​)e−μi​] at zero. The M-step maximizes a logistic log-likelihood with fractional responses τi​ and a Poisson log-likelihood with weights 1−τi​. With only a binary predictor, write nj​ for group size, Sj​=∑xi​=j​τi​ and Cj​=∑xi​=j​Yi​; the explicit updates are πj​=Sj​/nj​ and μj​=Cj​/(nj​−Sj​). Log and logit group contrasts recover the regression coefficients, with boundary values interpreted through limits.

Poisson central limit theorem OurBigBook.com
If Xλ​ has a Poisson distribution, then P(Xλ​≤⌊λ⌋)→1/2 as λ→∞. The Poisson central limit theorem standardizes by mean λ and variance λ; the cutoff (⌊λ⌋−λ)/λ​ tends to zero. Squeezing between fixed nearby cutoffs and using continuity of the standard normal distribution function gives the limit.

Poisson trick

Words: 148 Articles: 2
Poisson-multinomial conditioning OurBigBook.com
For each group g, let independent cell counts have Poisson means μgj​. Conditional on their total ng​, the cells have a multinomial distribution with probabilities
πgj​=∑k​μgk​μgj​​.
(48)
Including a free group main effect in the Poisson log-linear model makes its profiled likelihood for the remaining parameters proportional to the corresponding multinomial likelihood. The two fits therefore give the same fitted proportions and likelihood-ratio comparisons.

Words: 84 Articles: 1
Poisson trick OurBigBook.com
For positive group totals, the improper prior du/u on an independent Poisson baseline yields the multinomial likelihood kernel after integration. This prior is flat in logu. A proper finite-variance log-rate prior generally introduces an additional coefficient-dependent factor.
Gaussian log-rate correction to the Poisson trick (R(S)=EΓ(n,1)​e−(logV−logS)2/(2s2))
Words: 49
Flat log-rate marginalization gives the multinomial likelihood OurBigBook.com
A mean-zero normal distribution prior of variance s2 on the log baseline multiplies the multinomial kernel by the displayed correction, up to a constant independent of coefficients. The factor is not constant in S, so the posterior equivalence is approximate. Dominated convergence makes it tend to one as s2 tends to infinity.
